## Personality

Cheerful, chatty and incurably hopeful, he can sell a ribbon to a scarecrow. He takes in any creature that looks lost.

## Lore

Mott is the travelling pedlar who stops at the Sleepy Snail every summer, and he could sell a ribbon to a scarecrow. He has, in fact, once, in a field outside a village with a very dry sense of humour, and the farmer paid. He is forty-one, round-faced, cheerful, chatty and incurably hopeful, with a laugh you can hear across a market and a pack on his back that clanks when he walks. He takes in any creature that looks lost. He always has. This summer that has turned out to be most of his trouble, and most of his comfort.

### On the road

Mott was born on the road, more or less, to a pedlar called Peg who walked the royal roads with a pack twice his size and a voice that could be heard two fields off. He walked beside her from the time he could walk, learned to count in ribbons and to bargain in tin cups, and slept in more haylofts than he can remember. When Peg died, twenty-one years ago, he took up her pack and her round, and he has walked it every year since. He has no house. In winter he lodges wherever the snow catches him, and in summer he walks.

His round brings him to Kaldemor every summer, along the Royal Road from the west, to the Sleepy Snail, where Molly gives him the small room at the end with the crooked window, feeds him far too much, and writes his name on the folded list in her apron of travellers who have promised to stop on the way back. He stops on his way east and again on his way home, and he has never missed a summer. He sells tinware, cups, pans, ladles and lanterns that shine like new money, and ribbons in every colour he can get, and the children of Kaldemor have been known to wait at the Market steps for him.

### The Deepwood

This summer he never reached the Snail. On the last stretch of the road, where the farm track turns off toward the woods, he saw a fat cat trotting away from the farms toward the trees, looking, he says, entirely too pleased with herself to be anywhere near a wood. He went after her to carry her home. He followed her further than he meant to, then further than was sensible, and then the mist came down and he could no longer tell which way home was.

Somewhere deep in the Deepwood, under great blue-capped mushrooms, the Shrooms found him. They came in a crowd, bolder than any he had ever seen, tore his pack open and carried off every piece of tinware he owned, every cup, pan and lantern, anything that shone. They left the ribbons. Mott still does not know whether to be relieved or insulted.

He found shelter in an old woodcutters' hut in Breezy Hollow, a quiet corner of the Deepwood, with a sound roof, a spring nearby and a rusty tin of old meal on a shelf. The cat found him there the same evening, as if she had meant to all along. He has tried to walk out twice, and twice the mushrooms around the hollow have driven him back. He has been there three weeks.

### Company

A week ago, on a misty morning, a lamb came out of the trees and stood at the hut door, bleating: a small speckled lamb with a bent ear, much too young to be out alone. Mott took it in, of course. He has tied a blue ribbon round the lamb's neck and a red one round the cat's, so that, he says, they look like somebody's, which they plainly are. The lamb grazes the clearing, the cat hunts mice and brings him the best ones, and in the evenings he talks to them both about Molly's pies.

He does not know whose they are. He has decided that somebody somewhere is missing a lamb and a cat very badly, and that he is not leaving this hut without them.

### What he wants and fears

Mott wants to walk into the Sleepy Snail with a lamb under one arm and a cat under the other and see Molly's face. He would also like his tinware back, every cup of it. He is a little afraid, though he will not say it even to the cat, that the woods have changed for good, and that the roads he grew up on are not the roads he will grow old on.

### Hooks

A hunter searching the Deepwood might find Mott's torn pack strap among the blue caps, and then, deeper in, the hut and all three of them inside. Later, someone might follow the Shrooms to wherever they have carried his tinware, and bring back enough of it for Mott to set out his wares at the Snail again.
